source.title: Algorithm Development in Neural Networks: Insights from the Streaming Parity Task
source.authors: L. van Rossem; Andrew M. Saxe

record.tranche_reason: The study tests delayed generalization and a proposed mechanism on algorithmic tasks, but uses streaming parity, recurrent networks, and automaton/state-merger measurements rather than the original modular-arithmetic grokking setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own training/generalization results and state-merger measurements for recurrent networks, plus state-count results for transformers. Cited grokking results are not recorded as rows. The study does not directly measure a Fourier circuit, weight norms during training, or a delay-versus-training-set-size curve.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own training runs. RNNs on streaming parity show sudden generalization after a memorization-like tree phase. Internal automaton states merge as generalization emerges, and an initialization-scale sweep switches generalization on or off. This is a different method (RNN, length extrapolation, automaton extraction) aimed at delayed algorithmic generalization and its mechanism. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that RNNs on finite-automaton tasks develop algorithms in two phases: tree fitting, then state mergers, with a phase transition to infinite generalization under suitable training conditions (enough data, small init). They stress this happens 'not consistently', that redundant states are expected, and that the account fits transformers less well, where RNNs show an advantage for infinite generalization.
record.recipe_differences: Uses recurrent networks trained on streaming parity and automaton/state-merger analysis; also examines transformer state counts on modular subtraction and addition. It does not reproduce the original modular-arithmetic grokking procedure or its circuit-progress measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization and state mergers depend on initial weight scale and training-data fraction; the paper reports similar qualitative results with tanh activation and with a discontinuous output map, though the latter is noisier. For transformers, results differ by representation: attention shows merger-like patterns while hidden states do not show a clear pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: In a transformer on modular subtraction or addition (the original grokking task), hidden-layer state counts show no merge pattern. Attention, and weakly the value matrix, show split-then-merge patterns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The automaton state-merger account of delayed generalization transfers only partially to transformers on grokking tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Only representation pairs that agree on all future outputs merge (103460 of 103460), but not all agreeing pairs merge, leaving redundant states.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Implicit gradient-descent bias merges functionally equivalent states, producing generalizing but non-minimal algorithms.

fits_no_version.finding: A critical training-data fraction and init scale separate tree-fitting from generalization, without any regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A data-size threshold for algorithmic generalization can arise from implicit gradient-descent bias alone, without weight decay.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The theoretical account is explicitly simplified: it ignores higher-order and global interactions, architecture-specific inductive biases, regularization, and noise. Several supplementary outcomes are qualitative or figure-based, and the paper does not quantify how optimization delay changes with training-set size.

untested.parts: How the delay scales as the training set shrinks. A long gap between training saturation and generalization was not shown; generalization coincides with zero training loss.
Fourier or other named circuits. No quantitative evidence that the progress measure leads the validation jump by a measurable margin.
Non-algorithmic data, weight-norm control, and the length of the delay as a function of init scale (only whether generalization happens at convergence).
All. There is no weight decay, no circuit-efficiency comparison and no ungrokking. A data threshold appears, but via implicit gradient-descent bias.
All. Across-run algorithm identity was not tested; redundant states give equivalent but non-minimal automata.
All. Plain SGD without momentum or regularization is used, but optimizer or precision was never varied as a cause.

missing.what: The mean pairwise representational distance never decreases, so state mergers are not mere contraction. The drop in state count is explained by agreeing pairs diverging, then merging.
missing.locator: Appendix D.1 Fig. 12; D.4 Fig. 15; Sec. 5.3 Fig. 10

missing.what: Training uses plain SGD with no momentum or regularization, so the sudden generalization arises without adaptive optimizers or weight decay.

record.verdict_notes: Generalization here is length extrapolation on streaming parity, not held-out in-distribution pairs as in the original grokking setup. Several supporting results (random tasks, tanh, discontinuity, transformers) are qualitative and figure-based. V5 links were removed because no weight decay or efficiency mechanism was tested.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests delayed generalization on streaming parity and a data-fraction/initialization sweep, but does not report how the optimization delay scales as the training set shrinks.
It measures automaton/state mergers, not Fourier circuits or continuous progress measures that anticipate the generalization jump.
The initialization-scale effect is tested on algorithmic tasks only. Non-algorithmic data, weight norm, and a lazy-to-rich transition are not tested.
LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
The study varies dataset size and initialization scale, but does not test weight decay, a low-norm efficiency account, circuit efficiency, or ungrokking below a critical dataset size.
Whether separate runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm rather than algorithms depending on architecture or hyperparameters.
Adaptive-optimizer instabilities and floating-point/softmax artifacts as causes of grokking-like delays.

rows.subject: recurrent neural network (single fully connected recurrent layer)
rows.operation_detail: Train on all streaming-parity sequences up to length 10
rows.value: Training loss becomes zero; the paper says this occurs just before state mergers and generalization
rows.note: The paper describes the training loss reaching zero before the automaton begins merging states.
rows.check: This is the training-curve reference for V1, not V2. The text says generalization begins 'right when the training loss becomes zero', so the gap between saturation and generalization is short, not 'long after'.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V1: training loss reaches zero as state merging begins; generalization occurs when the automaton becomes finite. Training-accuracy saturation and the subsequent delay are not established.
source_check.problem: Zero training loss alone does not establish V1 or demonstrate that its post-saturation delay is short.

rows.subject: recurrent neural network (single fully connected recurrent layer)
rows.operation_detail: Track validation loss on sequences of different lengths during training
rows.value: figure only; the text says validation loss initially does not change, then suddenly drops for all sequence lengths
rows.note: The text describes a delayed, sudden improvement across the reported sequence lengths; numerical loss values are not stated.
rows.check: The sudden drop in validation loss is observed, but it coincides with training loss reaching zero rather than coming long after it. Validation here is length extrapolation (100 sequences of length 50, plus longer lengths in Fig. 6), not held-out in-distribution pairs.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V1: validation loss initially remains unchanged, then drops suddenly across sequence lengths. The text does not establish the interval from training-accuracy saturation to that drop.
source_check.problem: The sudden validation-loss drop is supported, but its coincidence with zero training loss is not explicitly established.

rows.subject: recurrent neural network (single fully connected recurrent layer)
rows.operation_detail: Extract automata from hidden representations during training
rows.baseline: initial automaton has few states and random outputs
rows.value: the automaton expands into a complete tree fitting the training data, then states merge until it becomes finite as generalization occurs
rows.note: The paper describes an initial tree-fitting phase followed by a state-merger/generalization phase.
rows.check: The automaton first forms a complete memorizing tree, then merges states until it is finite, which is when generalization occurs. This is the V2 pattern of memorize first, structure later, measured with an automaton state count rather than a Fourier circuit.

rows.subject: recurrent neural network
rows.operation_detail: Sweep initial weight scale and training-data fraction

conditions.value: initial weight scale and training dataset size

rows.value: a sudden jump from 0.5 to 1.0 at enough data and small enough initial weights
rows.note: The text states that all trials converged on the training set. The accuracy sweep varies both initialization scale and training-data fraction.
rows.check: This is accuracy at convergence across an initialization/data sweep, not a delay over training time, so it cannot show V1's delay. It bears on V3: small initial weights switch generalization on, and the authors liken this to rich vs lazy learning. It was removed from V5 because no weight decay or efficiency mechanism is involved.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V3: final validation accuracy switches from 0.5 to 1.0 with sufficient data and small initialization. The sweep does not measure delayed generalization or its timing.
source_check.problem: A generalization switch at convergence does not establish a switch in grokking-like delays.

rows.subject: recurrent neural network
rows.operation_detail: Sweep initial weight scale and training-data fraction

conditions.value: initial weight scale and training dataset size

rows.measure: number of automaton states at convergence
rows.value: figure only; the text says agreeing states begin to merge with smaller initialization scale or larger training set, and a sharp boundary separates tree-fitting from finite generalizing representations
rows.note: The paper links smaller initial weight scale and more datapoints to state mergers and the transition to a finite representation; exact state counts are not stated in the text.
rows.check: This is the final state count across the init-scale/data sweep: a finite automaton at small init versus a tree at larger init. It does not bear on V2's time course or on V5's weight-decay account.

relationships.reason: Validation loss is flat, then drops suddenly for all lengths, but this coincides with training loss reaching zero rather than coming long after it (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss remained flat before dropping suddenly across all tested lengths, while merger onset occurred at zero training loss.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: The text establishes merger onset at zero training loss and generalization upon finite-automaton formation, without establishing their temporal separation or training-accuracy saturation. It therefore does not demonstrate the claimed short or absent post-saturation delay; an unestablished timing component cannot justify limits_scope.

relationships.condition: RNNs on streaming parity and random regular tasks (ReLU, tanh, discontinuous output)
relationships.reason: A memorizing tree forms first, then gradual state mergers yield a finite automaton exactly when generalization occurs (r3, r8, r9, r10). The measure is an automaton state count, not a Fourier circuit.
relationships.display_finding: A memorizing tree forms first, then gradual state mergers produce a finite automaton exactly when generalization occurs.
